value.overview: The Blue Dacnis is a small, brightly colored tanager of tropical Central and South America. It usually occupies the forest canopy, where it searches among leaves, flowers, and fruiting branches. Males are vivid turquoise-blue and black, while females are mostly green with a bluish head. Agile and active, the species often travels in pairs, family parties, or mixed-species flocks. It is also called the Turquoise Honeycreeper.
value.classification: Scientific name: Dacnis cayana. It belongs to the tanager family, Thraupidae, within the order Passeriformes.
value.identification: The Blue Dacnis is about 12–13 cm long and has a short, pointed bill. Adult males are brilliant turquoise-blue with a black eye mask, throat, back, wings, and tail. Females are mainly bright green, with a blue-tinged head, paler underparts, and dark wings edged in green. Young birds resemble females, with young males gradually acquiring blue-and-black plumage. Both sexes have pinkish-red legs, although their color may appear duller under some conditions.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama into northern and central South America. Its range includes Trinidad and much of Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina. Blue Dacnises inhabit humid lowland and foothill forests, forest edges, secondary woodland, plantations, clearings with scattered trees, and well-vegetated gardens. They spend much of their time in the canopy and at fruiting or flowering trees.
value.migrationStatus: Primarily resident. Birds may make local or seasonal movements in response to flowering and fruiting plants.
value.breeding: Breeding timing varies across the species’ extensive tropical range. The female builds a small, neat cup nest from fine plant fibers and other soft material, usually placing it on a branch or among foliage above the ground. A typical clutch contains two or three eggs. The female performs most or all incubation, while the male may remain nearby and bring food. Both parents are reported to feed and attend the nestlings after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: Blue Dacnises eat small fruits, berries, nectar, and arthropods. They forage actively among outer branches and foliage, picking insects and spiders from leaves, twigs, and flowers. Their pointed bills help them inspect narrow spaces and take nectar from blossoms. They may hang upside down or stretch into unusual positions while feeding. Fruiting and flowering trees can attract several individuals along with other tanagers and canopy birds.
value.behavior: Usually seen in pairs, small groups, or mixed-species feeding flocks, the Blue Dacnis is quick-moving and acrobatic. It spends most of its time high in trees but may descend to forest edges, gardens, and low fruiting vegetation. Individuals make short flights between exposed branches and dense foliage while searching for food. Their calls are generally thin, high-pitched notes, and their song consists of light, varied whistles and twittering phrases.

conservation.populationTrend: Unknown; the global population has not been quantified reliably.
